name: Schloss Weiherburg
kurzbeschreibung: Schloss Weiherburg above Innsbruck: a Late Gothic noble manor from 1460, menagerie of Archduke Ferdinand II, St. Anne's castle chapel, and panoramic views of the city.
beschreibung:
Overview

The history-steeped Schloss Weiherburg is idyllically situated on the sunny southern slope of the Nordkette in the Hötting district of Innsbruck, roughly 100 meters above the Inn valley at an elevation of about 670 meters. Directly bordering the extensive Innsbruck Alpenzoo, this fortified Late Gothic noble manor is a popular excursion destination for culture enthusiasts and walkers. Surrounded by mature tree-lined avenues, orchards, and a castle pond, the estate offers one of the most magnificent panoramic vistas across the historic Altstadt of Innsbruck, the Inn River, and the glaciated peaks of the Stubai Alps.

Route & Requirements

The origins of Weiherburg date back to the 15th century: around the year 1460, Christian Tänzl, a wealthy saltworks and mining entrepreneur from Hall, commissioned this prestigious manor house. The Tänzl family, who had amassed immense fortune through silver mining in Schwaz, created a tower-like, fortified residence with crenellated walls. The castle derived its name from a fish pond (Weiher) created at that time. A defining turning point came in 1567: the art-loving Tyrolean sovereign Erzherzog Ferdinand II. acquired Weiherburg and gifted it to his morganatic wife Philippine Welser. Ferdinand had the building embellished with Renaissance wall frescoes and expanded the complex with the art-historically significant St.-Anna-Schlosskapelle, whose winged altarpiece and frescoes were created by Innsbruck court painter Meister Jörg. Furthermore, the sovereign laid out an expansive menagerie (Tiergarten) with rare animal species around the castle – this historic animal garden is considered the direct spiritual forerunner of today's Alpenzoo Innsbruck, founded in 1962. Following several changes of ownership, the castle was purchased in 1911 by the municipality of Innsbruck. After a comprehensive and painstaking restoration, the castle is now used as a stylish municipal reception venue as well as an acclaimed castle restaurant.

Visit & Arrival

The well-kept castle courtyard, panoramic viewing terraces, and outdoor grounds are freely accessible and free of charge throughout the entire year. The historic castle chapel can be viewed during events or by prior arrangement. The castle restaurant Weiherburg delights guests from Wednesday through Sunday with refined Tyrolean regional cuisine (closed Monday and Tuesday). Arriving by public transport: Take the modern Hungerburgbahn funicular from Innsbruck Congress or Löwenhaus to the Alpenzoo station; from there, a signposted walking path leads gently downhill directly to the castle in about five minutes. Alternatively, Innsbruck city bus line W runs directly to the Alpenzoo/Weiherburg stop. On foot, walk up from the city center (Hans-Psenner-Steg) in about 20 minutes via the shaded Weiherburgweg. By car: Paid parking is available at the large Alpenzoo parking area (Weiherburggasse).

Tips

The castle terrace and outer courtyard are level and readily navigable for strollers and wheelchairs; access to the castle inn is designed with minimal barriers. Ideally, combine your castle excursion with a visit to the adjacent Alpenzoo Innsbruck. Sitting on the wooden park benches beneath the ancient linden trees, visitors can enjoy an unforgettable play of light over the rooftops of the Tyrolean capital, particularly at dusk.
